items.claim: The hijack condition is a more-privileged process failing to find a DLL in all its earlier search locations and then falling through to a writable directory in the system PATH.
items.body:
The hijack condition is a more-privileged process failing to find a DLL in all its earlier search locations and then falling through to a writable directory in the system PATH.

HackTricks reference: writable sys path dll hijacking privesc (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HackTricks-wiki/hacktricks/master/src/windows-hardening/windows-local-privilege-escalation/dll-hijacking/writable-sys-path-dll-hijacking-privesc.md)
items.disproof: The DLL resolves in an earlier search location, or the system PATH contains no user-writable directory.

sources.quote: This can be abused through DLL hijacking when a more-privileged service or process tries to load a DLL that does not exist in its earlier search locations and eventually searches the writable system PATH directory.
The product uses a fixed or controlled search path to find resources, but one or more locations in that path can be under the control of unintended actors.

Other environment variables treated in this way include: GCONV_PATH , GETCONF_DIR , HOSTALIASES , LOCALDOMAIN , LD_AUDIT , LD_DEBUG , LD_DEBUG_OUTPUT , LD_DYNAMIC_WEAK , LD_HWCAP_MASK , LD_LIBRARY_PATH , LD_ORIGIN_PATH , LD_PRELOAD , LD_PROFILE , LD_SHOW_AUXV , LOCALDOMAIN , LOCPATH , MALLOC_TRACE , NIS_PATH , NLSPATH , RESOLV_HOST_CONF , RES_OPTIONS , TMPDIR , and TZDIR .

items.claim: For an unpackaged application on the standard search order, the system PATH is consulted only after redirection, API sets, SxS, the loaded-module list, KnownDLLs, the application and Windows directories, and the current directory all fail, which narrows hijack candidates to DLLs absent from every earlier location.

items.disproof: The target is a packaged application using redirection or API sets, so the system PATH is never reached.

items.claim: Trace service startup with Procmon to catch DLLs that are tried and not found, then check whether a user-writable directory sits in the Machine PATH; that pair is the hijack condition.
items.body:
Trace service startup with Procmon to catch DLLs that are tried and not found, then check whether a user-writable directory sits in the Machine PATH; that pair is the hijack condition.

items.disproof: No Machine PATH entry is user-writable, or no service attempts to load a DLL that is missing from all earlier search locations.

sources.quote:
To identify DLLs that services try and fail to load, launch Procmon as early as possible (before the processes start), then:

> [!WARNING]
> Adding a user-writable directory to the Machine PATH creates the vulnerable condition.
The product uses a fixed or controlled search path to find resources, but one or more locations in that path can be under the control of unintended actors.

Other environment variables treated in this way include: GCONV_PATH , GETCONF_DIR , HOSTALIASES , LOCALDOMAIN , LD_AUDIT , LD_DEBUG , LD_DEBUG_OUTPUT , LD_DYNAMIC_WEAK , LD_HWCAP_MASK , LD_LIBRARY_PATH , LD_ORIGIN_PATH , LD_PRELOAD , LD_PROFILE , LD_SHOW_AUXV , LOCALDOMAIN , LOCPATH , MALLOC_TRACE , NIS_PATH , NLSPATH , RESOLV_HOST_CONF , RES_OPTIONS , TMPDIR , and TZDIR .
